title: What is AQE (Adaptive Query Execution) — a Spark SQL optimization that uses runtime statistics to modify the physical plan during execution — and how does it complement (not replace) the Catalyst Optimizer?
shortTitle: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) and how it complements Catalyst

s1_definition.profdef: Adaptive Query Execution, or AQE, is a Spark SQL feature that re-optimizes the physical plan during execution using real statistics gathered from completed stages, rather than relying only on estimates made before the job runs. It works at shuffle boundaries, where accurate data about partition sizes becomes available, to coalesce small partitions, handle skewed partitions, and switch join strategies. AQE complements the Catalyst Optimizer rather than replacing it: Catalyst produces the initial optimized plan from static rules and estimates, and AQE refines that plan at runtime with facts.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India plans a report based on last year's guess of how many transactions each branch has. Catalyst is the planner who makes the best plan it can from those guesses before work begins. But guesses are often wrong — maybe one branch actually did ten times more transactions this month. AQE is like a supervisor standing at each checkpoint during the work, counting the actual files that just came through, and adjusting the remaining plan on the spot: merging tiny piles together, splitting one giant pile across more clerks, and even changing how two teams combine their work. Catalyst plans from estimates up front; AQE corrects the plan with real counts as the work happens.
s1_definition.oneliner: Catalyst optimizes the plan before execution using estimates, and AQE re-optimizes the physical plan during execution using real runtime statistics at shuffle boundaries — the two work together.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Adaptive Query Execution, or AQE, is a Spark SQL feature that re-optimizes the physical plan during execution using real statistics gathered from completed stages, rather than relying only on estimates made before the job runs. It works at shuffle boundaries, where accurate data about partition sizes becomes available, to coalesce small partitions, handle skewed partitions, and switch join strategies. AQE complements the Catalyst Optimizer rather than replacing it: Catalyst produces the initial optimized plan from static rules and estimates, and AQE refines that plan at runtime with facts.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India plans a report based on last year's guess of how many transactions each branch has. Catalyst is the planner who makes the best plan it can from those guesses before work begins. But guesses are often wrong — maybe one branch actually did ten times more transactions this month. AQE is like a supervisor standing at each checkpoint during the work, counting the actual files that just came through, and adjusting the remaining plan on the spot: merging tiny piles together, splitting one giant pile across more clerks, and even changing how two teams combine their work. Catalyst plans from estimates up front; AQE corrects the plan with real counts as the work happens.

**One line to remember:** Catalyst optimizes the plan before execution using estimates, and AQE re-optimizes the physical plan during execution using real runtime statistics at shuffle boundaries — the two work together.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem AQE solves is that the Catalyst Optimizer must commit to a physical plan before the job runs, using statistics that are often stale, missing, or wrong. It may not know the true size of a table after filtering, or that one key is wildly more common than others, or that a shuffle will produce many tiny partitions. These misestimates lead to poor choices: too many small tasks, one giant skewed task, or a shuffle join where a broadcast join would have been far cheaper.

AQE addresses this by making the physical plan adaptive. Execution proceeds stage by stage, and at each shuffle boundary the actual statistics of the just-completed shuffle become known — the real number and size of the output partitions. AQE pauses, reads those real statistics, and rewrites the remaining physical plan accordingly before launching the next stage. Because a shuffle is already a synchronization barrier, this re-optimization fits naturally at exactly those points and adds little overhead.

AQE has three headline optimizations, all driven by these runtime statistics. It coalesces small post-shuffle partitions, merging many tiny partitions into fewer appropriately sized ones so the next stage has fewer, better-balanced tasks. It handles skew by detecting oversized shuffle partitions and splitting them into smaller sub-partitions, so one hot key no longer creates a single long-running straggler task. And it dynamically switches join strategies, for instance converting a planned sort-merge shuffle join into a broadcast join once it discovers that one side is actually small enough to broadcast.

The crucial framing, and the part interviewers want, is that AQE complements and does not replace Catalyst. Catalyst still does all the up-front work: parsing, analysis, rule-based logical optimization like predicate pushdown and column pruning, and initial physical planning with cost-based strategy selection. AQE then layers on top, correcting the physical plan at runtime where static estimates were wrong. A senior nuance is that AQE is enabled by default in modern Spark, but it only helps where there are shuffles and real statistics to use, so it does not optimize a job with no shuffle, and it is not a substitute for good data layout, partitioning, or sometimes manual salting of extreme skew. In the bank, enabling AQE smoothed out exactly the problems our static plans could not anticipate — month-end spikes in one branch's data and joins whose sizes we could not predict.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The planner guessed partition sizes wrong, leaving many tiny partitions. This is exactly what AQE partition coalescing fixes using real counts.

Problem 2 — One branch unexpectedly produced a huge skewed partition. This is exactly what AQE skew handling splits apart.

Problem 3 — A table turned out much smaller after filtering than estimated. This is exactly what AQE dynamic join switching exploits by broadcasting.

The mini-project models AQE in Java. `CatalystPlan` holds an initial physical plan with estimated partition sizes and a planned join strategy. An `AqeReoptimizer` receives real runtime statistics after a simulated shuffle and rewrites the plan: coalescing small partitions, splitting a skewed one, and switching the join to broadcast when the real size is small. The demo runs a report over branch transaction counts for accounts belonging to Rajesh and Priya and prints the before-and-after plan.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Catalyst's initial plan says two hundred shuffle partitions and a sort-merge join, based on an estimate that the right side of the join is five hundred megabytes. The real post-shuffle statistics show three tiny branch partitions under one megabyte each, one skewed partition of one hundred twenty megabytes, and a real right side of only eight megabytes.

Step 1: The job runs the first stage and reaches the shuffle boundary, where the actual partition sizes and the real join side size become known. Catalyst's plan was made before this, so it could only guess.

Step 2: AQE reads the real statistics. It counts three partitions smaller than one megabyte, identifies the one-hundred-twenty-megabyte partition as skewed, and sees the real right side is eight megabytes.

Step 3: AQE applies partition coalescing, merging the three tiny partitions into fewer, so the next stage has far fewer, better-balanced tasks instead of many wasteful small ones.

Step 4: AQE applies skew handling, flagging the one-hundred-twenty-megabyte partition and splitting it into sub-partitions so one hot branch no longer causes a single long straggler task.

Step 5: AQE applies dynamic join switching. Because the real right side is eight megabytes, under the ten-megabyte broadcast threshold, it converts the planned sort-merge shuffle join into a broadcast join, eliminating a shuffle entirely.

Step 6: The final plan reflects all three corrections, something Catalyst alone could never have produced from its stale estimates. The journey shows Catalyst planning from guesses and AQE correcting with facts at the shuffle boundary.

```text
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] Catalyst initial plan: partitions=200, join=SORT_MERGE
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE: reading real runtime statistics at the shuffle boundary
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE coalesce: merged 3 tiny partitions => 2 partitions
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [WARNING] AQE skew: partition 'HYD' is 120000000 bytes — splitting into sub-partitions
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE join switch: real right side 8000000 bytes <= 10MB => switch SORT_MERGE to BROADCAST (no shuffle)
2026-10-30 03:41:00 [INFO] AQE final plan: partitions=2, join=BROADCAST
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  Catalyst (before run, from ESTIMATES): 200 partitions, SORT_MERGE join
    │
    ▼  execute stage 1 → reach SHUFFLE BOUNDARY (real stats now known)
  Runtime stats: [MUM 0.8MB, DEL 0.6MB, BLR 0.9MB, HYD 120MB], rightSide=8MB
    │
    ▼  AQE re-optimizes the REMAINING physical plan:
    ├─ coalesce small partitions   (3 tiny → merged)
    ├─ split skewed partition      (HYD 120MB → sub-partitions)
    └─ switch join strategy        (SORT_MERGE → BROADCAST, right side 8MB)
    │
    ▼
  Final adaptive plan: 2 partitions, BROADCAST join  (Catalyst + AQE together)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Adaptive Query Execution, or AQE, is a Spark SQL feature that re-optimizes the physical plan during execution using real statistics gathered from completed stages, instead of relying only on the estimates made before the job runs. The problem it solves is that the Catalyst Optimizer has to commit to a physical plan up front using statistics that are often stale, missing, or simply wrong — it may not know the true size of a table after filtering, or that one key is far more common than others, or that a shuffle will produce many tiny partitions. Those misestimates lead to too many small tasks, a single giant skewed task, or a shuffle join where a broadcast join would have been far cheaper.

AQE fixes this by making the plan adaptive at shuffle boundaries, which is exactly where accurate statistics become available and where there is already a synchronization barrier, so re-optimization fits naturally and adds little overhead. It has three headline optimizations: it coalesces many small post-shuffle partitions into fewer, better-balanced ones; it detects oversized skewed partitions and splits them so a hot key no longer creates a straggler; and it dynamically switches join strategies, for example converting a planned sort-merge shuffle join into a broadcast join once it learns one side is actually small. The framing I always stress is that AQE complements Catalyst rather than replacing it — Catalyst still does parsing, analysis, rule-based logical optimization like predicate pushdown and column pruning, and initial physical planning, and AQE then corrects that physical plan at runtime where the static estimates were wrong.

In my project at the National Bank of India, enabling AQE smoothed out precisely the problems our static plans could not anticipate. Month-end spikes in a single branch's transactions used to create skewed partitions and long straggler tasks, and AQE's skew splitting handled that automatically. Joins whose post-filter sizes we could not predict were sometimes silently converted to broadcast joins, removing shuffles we would otherwise pay for. The one caution I add is that AQE only helps where there are shuffles and real statistics to use, so it does not optimize a shuffle-free job, and it is not a substitute for good data layout, sensible partitioning, or occasionally salting extreme skew by hand.
